extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, newsroom managers, fact-checkers and media-watchers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and norms for issuing, wording and handling corrections in news organizations — when to correct, how to explain errors, and how to avoid/rectify systemic reporting failures. Emphasizes transparency, prominence, and remediation for serious mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections policy existence and value
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections policies are an unequivocally good thing about journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publications should have and follow transparent corrections policies; the piece repeatedly praises outlets that correct themselves and links to past annual correction roundups as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and completeness (no stealth edits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should value publications that honestly correct themselves over those that pretend nothing happened or stealthily edit past mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections should be explicit rather than quietly changing the text; visible acknowledgement preserves trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about the reporting process and how the error occurred
rubrics_metrics.description: A correction should 'shed light on the reporting process that led to the mistake' and explain the chain of reporting, sources used, and assumptions made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correction to explain which sources informed the original story, what was assumed (e.g., misreading redactions or ambiguous wording), and why that led to the error — as ProPublica did in a long corrective note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and apology when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms should take responsibility for errors and be equally accountable as they hold others to account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections can include explicit statements of responsibility or regret; the ProPublica example frames the outlet accepting accountability and apologizing for muddling an important national debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate by severity (categorize corrections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all corrections are equal — distinguish between trivial/funny errors and serious errors that reveal systemic bias or severe mispractice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article groups corrections into 'funny', 'weird' and 'serious' categories; serious corrections warrant fuller explanations and potentially further newsroom action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive corrections for high-impact errors
rubrics_metrics.description: When errors materially mislead public debate or combine contentious storylines, corrections should be substantial, detailed and public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lengthy, explicit corrections (with context and sourcing) are appropriate for stories that had broad impact or involved contested facts, as in the ProPublica and The Intercept examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of photos and user-generated content before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Miscaptioned photos and unvetted user-generated content are common markers of poor verification and of 'fake news' operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms must verify timestamps, origins and context of images and UGC to avoid using outdated or unrelated photos (examples: Arizona Republic using 2014 photos; Fox News using unrelated footage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat satire as factual reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlets must verify whether content originates from satirical sites before treating it as real news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove or correct material mistakenly attributed to a satirical web publication (example: Washington Post removing material from Clickhole).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely correction and headline/story updates
rubrics_metrics.description: When headlines or key story elements are incorrect, update them promptly and note the correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New York Times example of dramatically changing a headline and issuing corrections shows headlines should be corrected as well as body text; note when and how the update was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence and placement of corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections should be issued prominently (print and/or online) rather than hidden in obscure locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections in follow-up print editions or clear online notices (e.g., 'We regret running an incorrect caption... We will issue a correction in tomorrow's paper.') increase visibility and reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge systemic or structural causes (e.g., lack of diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious errors that recur (e.g., wrong photos of Black public figures) may stem from systemic newsroom issues that should be acknowledged and addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond fixing the immediate error, newsrooms should investigate and work toward structural remedies such as improving diversity, training and workflows to prevent repeat mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact sources and document follow-up efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections should describe efforts to contact sources and any limitations encountered (e.g., declined comment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailing who was contacted and when — and noting when sources decline to comment — helps explain why the original error happened and what steps were taken during correction (see ProPublica contacting Mitchell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misidentifying individuals; exercise care in identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful identification of people and photos is essential to avoid embarrassing or harmful misidentifications (e.g., confusing public figures or using the wrong obituary photo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement verification steps for names, photos and roles; repeated failures (mixing up people with similar names, using an unrelated photo for an obituary) indicate procedural breakdowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use corrections to rebuild trust and demonstrate editorial standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing honest corrections contributes to press freedom and reader trust; corrections are part of accountability and quality control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing corrections as part of a commitment to accuracy and transparency — and inviting reader scrutiny/support — reinforces credibility (the piece asks readers to value outlets that correct themselves).
